content.rationale: Bottleneck Mahalanobis distance is sensitive to nearby held-out intents, while encoder-space distance captures broader domain shifts. Training-set dispersion calibrates their additive weights without using evaluation statistics.

ViM-style residual magnitude measures how far an encoder representation lies outside the principal subspace occupied by training intents. OOS queries often retain a larger component in these discarded directions than in-scope queries.

A multiscale nearest-neighbour distance combines local novelty with broader training-manifold sparsity. OOS queries should be distant from both their closest examples and moderately sized neighborhoods of in-scope training queries.

Trailing within-class covariance directions emphasize low-variance features that in-scope examples tightly constrain. OOS queries can have unusually large residual energy in these directions even when their dominant semantic components resemble an intent.

A query can be near an in-scope centroid yet be implausible for the class selected by the classifier. The predicted-class Mahalanobis tail probability measures disagreement between the classifier decision and class-conditional representation geometry.

In-scope predictions typically have class-specific logit concentration and a stable top-two separation. Queries with unusually diffuse, low-margin logits relative to training examples assigned to the same predicted class are more likely to be out-of-scope.

L2-normalized bottleneck features remove representation magnitude and measure angular agreement with each intent prototype. OOS queries should have lower cosine similarity to every training class prototype than in-scope examples.

Energy and full encoder-space Mahalanobis distance capture complementary classifier uncertainty and representation atypicality. Empirical train-distribution calibration puts both signals on a common robust scale without using evaluation-set statistics.

The normalized Dirichlet concentration vector describes how evidence is distributed among intents independently of total evidence (vacuity). OOS queries often have unusually diffuse evidence shapes for their predicted intent, so a class-conditional lower-tail score of Dirichlet concentration is high.

Confident in-scope predictions retain the energy ordering, while high-energy uncertain predictions are increasingly scored by encoder-space atypicality. This conditional blend uses feature distance only where classifier confidence is insufficient.

Class-specific diagonal variances capture intent-dependent feature dispersion that a tied covariance misses. Shrinkage toward the global variance keeps rare-intent covariance estimates stable while exposing atypical queries.

The span of class means captures directions that distinguish known intents, while residual encoder energy measures variation not explained by those discriminative directions. OOS queries should retain more energy in this class-mean-orthogonal remainder.

Bottleneck and encoder densities capture near-intent and broad domain novelty respectively. Each density is converted to its training empirical lower-tail probability before additive fusion, preventing either representation's raw distance scale from dominating.

A classifier-selected intent may be close to its centroid while still lying outside that intent's local principal subspace. Class-conditional residual energy detects this off-manifold novelty and is calibrated against residuals of training examples from the same predicted intent.

Classifier-selected class-conditional neighbourhood distance detects queries that may be near the overall training manifold but are not locally supported by examples of the intent the classifier predicts. L2-normalized encoder representations emphasize semantic angular similarity rather than feature magnitude.
The fraction of within-class residual energy lying in trailing covariance directions emphasizes constraints that in-scope representations satisfy tightly while discounting broad feature magnitude.

In-scope representations tend to have a clearly preferred class centroid, whereas OOS queries are often both far from known centroids and geometrically ambiguous between multiple intents. A nearest-versus-second-nearest Mahalanobis margin supplements absolute representation atypicality without relying on classifier logits.
The top-two logit margin measures class-decision ambiguity independently of the overall logit offset captured by energy; OOS queries often have unusually small margins.

Cosine agreement with the prototype of the classifier-selected intent detects representations whose predicted label is not supported by the corresponding angular feature geometry. Class-conditional training calibration makes low agreement unusual relative to examples receiving the same predicted intent.
Classifier uncertainty and classifier-selected feature-space mismatch are calibrated within predicted intents, then combined on a common empirical tail scale.

The normalized Dirichlet concentration vector captures the relative allocation of evidential mass across intents while discarding total concentration and vacuity. An OOS query can have a familiar predicted class but an evidence-allocation shape atypical of training queries assigned to that class.

Energy remains the score for training-like confident predictions, while a train-calibrated encoder Mahalanobis correction is activated only for low-confidence predictions. This targets queries whose classifier uncertainty makes representation atypicality especially informative.

Intent classes can have substantially different feature dispersions, so classifier-selected diagonal Gaussian surprise with sample-size shrinkage can expose queries that are implausible for their predicted intent. Per-class empirical calibration removes density offsets caused by differing class volumes.

Removing the class-mean discriminative subspace leaves variation that is weakly explained by known intent separation. OOS queries should have poorly supported local neighborhoods in this residual representation even when their discriminative projection resembles an in-scope intent.

A global principal subspace captures dominant in-scope encoder variation, while the residual norm measures representation energy unsupported by that manifold. Adding a train-scaled residual correction to energy implements a ViM-style novelty signal.

Averaging an annulus of normalized bottleneck-space neighbour distances measures sustained local support rather than relying on one accidentally close training example. OOS queries should have consistently weaker semantic neighbourhood support across these scales.
Known intents are tightly constrained along trailing within-class covariance directions, so whitened residual energy in those low-variance directions exposes off-manifold OOS queries.

In-scope representations should usually have a clearly preferred class centroid, whereas OOS queries can be similarly distant from multiple known intents. A small nearest-versus-second-nearest Mahalanobis gap therefore indicates geometric class ambiguity rather than merely global distance.

The centered logit norm measures decisiveness of the full relative logit configuration while removing the common logit offset that drives energy. OOS queries may have unusually weak class-separating evidence even when their absolute logit scale is unremarkable.

Energy captures classifier-level uncertainty while encoder Mahalanobis distance captures representation novelty. Calibrating both against their respective training distributions puts their tail evidence on a common scale before fusion.

The collision entropy of normalized Dirichlet concentrations measures how diffusely evidence is allocated across intents, independent of total evidential mass. OOS queries should have unusually diffuse allocation relative to training queries predicted as the same intent.

Confident items retain the energy ordering, while items with unusually high energy smoothly transition toward encoder-space Mahalanobis novelty. This lets feature distance dominate only in the uncertain regime where logits are less reliable.
A classifier prediction that disagrees with the nearest class under class-specific shrunk diagonal variances indicates feature-to-logit inconsistency that is uncommon in scope.

Known intents can exhibit predictable residual encoder variation conditioned on their most discriminative class-mean coordinates. OOS queries should have large class-predicted residual reconstruction errors even when their projection onto discriminative directions appears plausible.

After removing the intent centroid, in-scope encoder representations should lie near a shared low-dimensional within-intent manifold. OOS queries retain unusually large residual energy outside that learned manifold even when a classifier assigns them a known intent.

Local support in a PCA-compressed pooled encoder space captures semantic novelty while suppressing noisy high-dimensional directions. The 30th normalized neighbour distance requires sustained support from known in-scope examples rather than one unusually close match.

Within-class trailing covariance directions represent tightly constrained variation that is largely ignored by dominant semantic factors. The largest standardized deviation in this low-variance subspace detects concentrated off-manifold departures from known intents.

Angular distance to the classifier-predicted intent prototype tests whether an embedding points in the semantic direction typical of that intent. Per-predicted-class robust scaling accommodates intents with different directional dispersion.

The top-two logit margin measures how decisively the classifier separates its selected intent from its nearest alternative, independently of the common logit offset captured by energy. OOS queries may retain high absolute logits yet show unusually weak relative intent separation.

Class-conditional empirical tail calibration makes logit uncertainty and distance-to-the-predicted-intent comparable despite different intent-specific score ranges. Fisher-style aggregation highlights queries that are unusually uncertain, geometrically implausible, or both.

Dirichlet mutual information measures disagreement between the predictive categorical distribution and class probabilities sampled from the evidential posterior. OOS inputs should induce epistemic uncertainty through low or unevenly distributed evidence, which is not a monotone function of vacuity or energy.

Classifier energy remains the novelty score for softmax-confident queries, preserving its useful ordering there. For classifier-uncertain queries, distance to the classifier-predicted class prototype supplies a geometry-based fallback.

Per-intent diagonal variance identifies coordinates where an intent permits little variation. Averaging the largest class-normalized coordinate residuals detects sparse off-manifold departures that a summed Mahalanobis score can dilute.

Class-mean directions encode variation that distinguishes known intents, so the encoder energy left orthogonal to that discriminative subspace measures semantic variation unsupported by the classifier's intent structure. Training-calibrated residual energy highlights queries that cannot be explained by known intent-separating factors.

A ViM-style residual norm captures encoder components unsupported by the dominant in-scope feature subspace, while energy captures classifier uncertainty. Training-calibrated addition combines semantic off-manifold evidence with weak intent evidence.

Average local support in the fine-tuned bottleneck space measures whether an input lies near a sustained neighborhood of known intent examples. L2 normalization emphasizes learned representation direction and reduces sensitivity to embedding magnitude.
Within-class trailing covariance directions are tightly constrained for known intents, so aggregate standardized residual energy in those directions exposes off-manifold OOS inputs.

In-scope embeddings usually have a clearly preferred Gaussian intent region, whereas OOS queries can be geometrically ambiguous between multiple class regions. A small gap between the nearest and second-nearest class Mahalanobis distances therefore indicates OOS risk.

After removing the common logit offset captured by energy, in-scope intents tend to have class-characteristic relative-logit norms. Atypical centered-logit concentration for the predicted intent signals OOS risk.

Cosine alignment with a known-intent prototype measures whether a bottleneck representation points in a direction supported by that intent. Calibrating the alignment relative to the predicted class's training distribution accounts for intent-specific prototype dispersion and avoids a globally equivalent raw-cosine ranking.

MSP uncertainty and pooled-space Mahalanobis distance capture complementary failure modes: an OOS query may be classifier-uncertain, geometrically atypical, or both. Training empirical percentiles put both signals on a common tail-probability scale, and their product emphasizes jointly unsupported inputs.

The normalized entropy of Dirichlet concentration proportions measures whether evidential mass is diffusely spread across intents, independently of its total amount. OOS queries may produce less intent-specific concentration shapes even when vacuity or energy alone is uninformative.

Energy remains the score for classifier-confident inputs, preserving its useful ordering there. A training-calibrated uncertainty gate shifts uncertain inputs toward pooled-space Mahalanobis distance, where geometric novelty can disambiguate unreliable logits.

Known intents should concentrate a substantial fraction of their bottleneck representation in directions that separate class means. A high class-calibrated fraction of energy remaining outside this discriminative subspace indicates variation unsupported by the learned intent structure.

In-scope encoder representations should lie close to the dominant principal subspace learned from training queries. Residual energy outside that subspace measures semantic variation unsupported by known intents without relying on classifier confidence.

The mean distance to several nearby training queries estimates local in-scope support more robustly than a single neighbor. Fine-tuned bottleneck directions should cluster by known intent, while OOS queries tend to have weak multi-neighbor support.

Low-variance within-class eigen-directions represent tightly constrained semantic variation, so a large excursion in even one such direction is evidence against known-intent support. Class-conditional calibration prevents naturally broader intents from being penalized as strongly.

OOS queries can be poorly supported by the classifier-predicted intent even when they are near some other intent region. A predicted-class residual calibrated per predicted intent, combined with disagreement against the nearest class region, exposes this mismatch.

The top-two gap after removing the common logit offset and normalizing logit magnitude measures intent-specific logit shape rather than confidence scale. OOS inputs with ambiguous class evidence should have unusually small predicted-class-calibrated normalized margins.

Known queries should have cosine similarity to their classifier-predicted intent prototype that exceeds similarity to competing intent prototypes. A low, class-calibrated prototype-agreement margin indicates semantic mismatch with the assigned intent.

Training empirical CDFs place logit uncertainty and pooled-space class distance on a shared in-scope tail scale. Taking the larger calibrated anomaly score detects queries that are unsupported either by classifier evidence or by intent geometry.

The centered log-ratio shape of Dirichlet concentrations captures relative evidence allocation across intents while removing total evidential mass. In-scope queries should match the class-specific evidence shape learned from training data, whereas OOS queries can have atypical concentration profiles.
Energy is retained as a monotone confidence score for training-supported, confident predictions, while a train-calibrated gate routes energy-uncertain queries toward pooled-space class distance.

Class-mean directions capture the feature variation most useful for separating known intents. After removing that discriminative component, unusually large class-calibrated residual variation indicates unsupported semantic content.

ViM-style residual norms measure feature content outside the dominant in-scope representation subspace. Adding a train-calibrated residual anomaly to energy detects inputs that are confident yet geometrically unsupported.

Averaging distances to multiple nearby normalized pooled embeddings estimates local in-scope support more smoothly than a single-neighbor radius. OOS queries should have consistently more distant local neighborhoods even when one accidental neighbor is close.
Trailing within-class covariance directions encode tightly constrained semantic variation, so unusually large low-variance residuals indicate unsupported intent content.

The centered logit norm measures concentration of intent evidence while removing the arbitrary common logit offset. OOS queries often have unusually weak class-discriminative evidence, producing a low norm relative to training items assigned to the same intent.
L2-normalized bottleneck features from known intents should align with their class prototype. Low cosine similarity to the classifier-predicted prototype indicates unsupported intent geometry.

Energy and bottleneck-space class distance capture complementary classifier uncertainty and geometric novelty. Mapping each score through its training empirical CDF and then to normal quantiles puts their in-scope tail behavior on a common, robust scale before combining them.
